newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bond yields down, brace for U.S. jobs.
newsitem.headline: Australian bond yields down, brace for U.S. jobs.

text.p: *Australian bond yields ended lower as the market squared up ahead of the key U.S. non-farm payrolls report and after a volatile trading week which saw easing hopes evaporate.
*Local jobs data, RBA board meeting next week.
Australian bond yields ended lower as the market squared up ahead of the key U.S. April non-farm payrolls report and after a volatile trading week which saw local easing hopes evaporate.

A slightly weaker than expected outcome to monthly and quarter retail trade data failed to make much impression on a market that has seen a slim chance of an easing evaporate after this week's strong wages data.
"Rate cut speculation remains on the back burner following the data on retail spending for March," said Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial State Bank.
"Following firm gains in spending in January and February, a more significant fall in sales would have been required to revive speculation over lower interest rates," added Kunnen.

March retail trade fell 0.3 percent after an expected flat outcome, while on the quarter it rose 2.2 percent versus an expected 2.4 percent, although it is still expected to add 0.5 percent to the first quarter GDP.
There had been speculation that weak data this week would have prompted thoughts of an easing when the Reserve Bank board meets for its monthly meeting next Tuesday.

"With the data released this week showing surprisingly strong wages growth, a rebound in building approvals for private sector houses and a surge in retail spending, an interest rate cut now seems a far more unlikely propect than at the beginning of the week," said Andrew Pease, senior economist at Nomura Australia.
No economist expected a change in policy in May and a majority expect the next move to be a tightening in the first quarter of 1998, according to Reuters monthly Australian interest rate poll.
The focus is now squarely on the U.S.
Forecasts are for a 211,000 rise in U.S. payrolls after a 175,000 in March, keeping the unemployment rate at 5.2 percent.
The local market retraced some ground against the U.S. after Thursday's spread blow-out, but the 10-year yield differenttial is still well above levels seen a week earlier.
